title: Come with me if you want ABS! (6 PACK MASSterplan)
summary: A three-step abs plan. Step 1 is one stretch-based exercise (sit-ups) for 6-9 sets a week, unweighted for max reps. Step 2 keeps the volume the same and adds weight within an 8-12 or 10-15 rep range. Step 3 adds a second exercise and goes up to 9-15 sets. He argues abs come from consistent, progressive training, not from cutting or gimmick routines, and that sit-ups are safe.
claims: Abs sit in the middle of everything, so weak abs make the whole physique look worse and a good core makes everything look better
Thinking you can only have a six-pack by getting very lean is a myth; you need to train the abs properly
Follow the plan for a year and you will at least have the start of a six-pack
Step 1: one stretch-based ab exercise for 6-9 sets a week total, spread over the week, never all on one day; 1-4 sets per session
Do not do more than 6-9 sets at first: previously untrained abs respond massively to little direct work
Two-week daily ab challenges fail; 6 sets a week for a year is 312 sets, which beats 15 sets a day for two weeks
The exercise is the sit-up: pelvis and feet fixed while the whole spine flexes and extends; floor, decline bench, GHR all fine
Crunches only flex the thoracic spine with no stretch and are worthless for hypertrophy
Beginners who can't brace may split volume with planks (e.g. 3 stretch + 3 plank sets); advanced lifters get enough isometric work from heavy compounds
In step 1 do sit-ups unweighted for as many reps as possible, without counting reps, to build mind-muscle connection and avoid rushing form
Progressive overload is a loaded rifle: use only as many bullets as you need and keep added weight in reserve
Move to step 2 when reps become ridiculous and you feel you could do sit-ups indefinitely
Step 2: same exercise, rep range 8-12 or 10-15, add weight when you max out the range
Superset ab work early in the session with upper-body lifts so it can't be skipped; avoid supersetting with heavy squats or deadlifts
In step 2 do not add sets: added weight makes up for the reduced volume
An extra 5-10 lb on sit-ups is like an extra 40 lb on squats for the abs
Weighted ab work can impair core rigidity; avoid it the day before heavy lower-body sessions, or do it at the end of leg days
Step 3: when progress stalls, add a second stretch-based exercise and train 9-15 sets a week split evenly
For details: windshield wipers for obliques, decline sit-ups with rotation for serratus, leg/knee raises with pelvic movement for lower abs
Don't pick more than two ab exercises; spinal flexion trains the whole core anyway
He stays at step 3 himself: 9-15 sets a week of sit-ups and leg raises, no more than 12 sets
Sit-ups are safe when done properly; pain points to a problem elsewhere. If flexion hurts, use hanging leg raises, which decompress the spine
exercises: feet fixed, full spinal flexion and extension, slow
only for beginners learning to brace
lower abs; replacement if flexion hurts
